newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Cavallo claims new proof of Argentine corruption.
newsitem.headline: Cavallo claims new proof of Argentine corruption.

text.p: Former Argentine Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo said he presented a 400-page file to back up charges that "mafias," or crime rings, were trying to control the mail service, and threatened to sue judges if they fail to investigate.
In a taped television interview broadcast late Thursday, Cavallo said that earlier in the week he presented Judge Jorge Urso with new evidence to substantiate his accusations.

Cavallo, who last July was fired by President Carlos Menem after six years in the cabinet, a year ago spent 15 hours in Congress denouncing "mafias" in power that he said were trying to control the postal service, which is being privatized.
Cavallo then accused private postal service businessman Alfredo Yabran of being behind the mafias and Yabran sued him for slander.

But Cavallo, the architect of a plan that returned Argentina to a path of economic growth and currency stability, now said he would prove his charges. "If there is justice in Argentina, Yabran should go to jail," he said.
The former minister also accused judges -- some of whom he has described as lackeys of the administration -- of dragging their feet in probing corruption cases.
"Now the culprits won't be able to get away so easily. The proof is there and if the judges and prosecutors don't go ahead and investigate, I will sue them for a cover-up."
In a telephone interview with the same talk show, Yabran's lawyer dismissed Cavallo's documents as "more of the same".

The former minister also lashed out at another federal judge, Guillermo Tiscornia, who is probing charges of massive smuggling and who on Wednesday ordered a police raid on the offices of a brother of Cavallo.

A police crackdown last month revealed a major "parallel customs service" run by crooked officials that smuggled goods into Argentina worth about $10 billion, costing the state $3.0 billion in lost customs duties.
Cavallo, who has also denounced corruption at the customs service, said it was typical of that judge to investigate the accusers rather than the accused whenever corruption charges were made.

The man who was Cavallo's customs chief, Gustavo Parino, is under investigation and Tiscornia said the raid on Jorge Cavallo's consulting firm, in which no arrests were made, showed he sent Parino a detailed report in 1994 on the risk of customs graft.
